summary:
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D scrollytelling website that presents NASA’s abandoned lunar and Martian hardware as an archaeological record. Scrolling carries the visitor from Earth orbit to the Moon, deep space, Mars and a “blueprint vault” of cancelled and lost missions. Along the way, each spacecraft gets its own illustrated schematic and a hands-on interaction. Examples are firing a laser at Apollo 11’s retroreflector, burying InSight’s solar panels in dust, and watching the Mars Climate Orbiter’s unit error send it off course. A searchable Master Archive of 14 missions lets users filter by world and by how each mission ended.

It addresses the challenge by turning scattered mission data into a story people can explore and compare. It matters because these spacecraft are heritage sites and engineering lessons, not space junk. They show how far hardware can outlast its mission, how avoidable errors end missions, and why we should document and preserve humanity’s first footprints on other worlds.
details:
Project title: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten

What it does and how it works

Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a 3D scrollytelling website that treats NASA’s abandoned lunar and Martian hardware as an archaeological record. As the visitor scrolls, a fixed Three.js scene carries them from Earth orbit to the Moon, through deep space, to Mars and finally into a “blueprint vault.” A persistent HUD (heads-up display) shows scroll progress, distance from Earth, the active sector and the mission era. A bottom-left ticker shows fictional “deep space network” comms messages.

The story is told in six scenes:

  1. Earth: the hook, with animated counters for 70+ years of exploration and 220+ tons of hardware left behind.
  2. The Moon: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 descent stage and its laser retroreflector, the Apollo lunar rovers, and the 2024 Odysseus lander.
  3. Deep space: the Pioneer plaques and the Kepler and Dawn spacecraft.
  4. Mars: Viking, Sojourner and Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, and the Ingenuity helicopter.
  5. Blueprint Vault: hardware that was cancelled or lost, including the VIPER rover, Mars Climate Orbiter and Apollo 18–20.
  6. Epilogue: a Master Archive of 14 missions.

Each mission has its own hand-built SVG schematic with a small interaction that explains what happened to it. Examples:

  • A Surveyor 3 toggle shows the parts Apollo 12 astronauts brought home.
  • A laser button fires a pulse at the Apollo 11 retroreflector.
  • A tilt slider shows how Odysseus ended up on its side.
  • A dust-storm control scrubs through Opportunity’s 2018 optical-depth readings.
  • An InSight dust slider shows its solar panels being buried.
  • A Mars Climate Orbiter toggle switches between imperial and metric thruster units.

The Master Archive lets visitors search the 14 missions and filter them by celestial body and by end-of-mission mode. The filters cover battery/cold, dust/solar, mechanical/impact, software/comms and budget/cancelled. Each result opens a detailed dossier with coordinates, mass, planned versus actual lifespan, and the last signal received.

Benefits

  • It turns dry mission data into a story people want to scroll through, so it works for students, space enthusiasts and general audiences.
  • It highlights a lesson that’s easy to miss: many of these spacecraft outlived their planned missions many times over, and others failed for avoidable reasons such as unit mismatches, budget cuts and dust.
  • It collects scattered mission history into one searchable, comparable archive.
  • It runs entirely in the browser, with no install or account needed.
  • A performance mode lets lower-powered devices run it smoothly.

Intended impact

We want people to see these spacecraft as heritage sites and time capsules rather than space junk. The project invites viewers to think about preserving planetary heritage and what future “space archaeologists” might find. It also shows how engineering failures, from the Mars Climate Orbiter unit error to cancelled missions, can teach us something.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Libraries: Three.js (r128) for the 3D scene, GSAP with ScrollTrigger for scroll-driven animation, and Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • Browser features: the Web Audio API for synthesized telemetry beeps and audio cues, and SVG and CSS animation for the interactive schematics.
  • Fonts: Google Fonts (Orbitron, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono, Inter).
  • AI: we used Gemini to help develop the project. (Add one line saying what you used it for, such as code, content research or ideas, in case the challenge asks you to disclose AI use.)
  • Hardware: a standard laptop or desktop. It needs only a modern WebGL-capable browser, with no special hardware.

How it’s creative

  • It’s built as a mission-control interface, with live-style telemetry, a signal ticker and a “Deep Space Network” HUD, instead of a standard article layout.
  • The scroll itself is the spacecraft: scrolling moves you through the solar system, and the background scene, colors and mood change with each world.
  • Every spacecraft has its own illustrated schematic and a small hands-on interaction.
  • The Blueprint Vault switches to a cyan CAD look to mark hardware that never flew.
  • Synthesized audio adds atmosphere without any audio files to load.
  • The Master Archive gives a data-driven way to compare missions beyond the narrative.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: mission facts, dates, masses, coordinates and failure causes are drawn from NASA and mission records, with checkable figures shown on each card.
  • Performance: a performance toggle and a lightweight 3D scene (simple geometry and particle points rather than heavy models) keep the frame rate usable on weaker devices.
  • Accessibility and usability: audio is off by default, there are quick-jump links in the HUD, and the layout is responsive.
  • Pacing: the story moves from wonder (Earth, Moon) to loss (Mars, dust, cancellations) to reflection (the epilogue manifesto).
  • Scope: we chose 14 well-documented missions across the Moon, Mars, deep space and cancelled programs so that each one could get proper attention.
